Content:
Recall that, in a directed graph [MATH: G=(V,E),] the indegree of a vertex is the number of incoming edges, while the outdegree is the number of outgoing edges.

Content:
A directed graph is called a regular directed graph if all its vertices have the same indegree and outdegree, and [MATH: k]-regular if that degree is [MATH: k]. In other words, a [MATH: k]-regular directed graph satisfies
[MATH: \deg^-(v_i)=\deg^+(v_i)=k]
for all [MATH: v_i\in V] and some fixed constant [MATH: k,] and a regular directed graph is a directed graph which is [MATH: k]-regular for some [MATH: k].

Content:
For example, consider the regular directed graphs shown below: in the graph on the left, each vertex has an indegree and an outdegree of [MATH: 2,] while in the graph on the right, each vertex has an indegree and an outdegree of [MATH: 1.]

[IMG: /graphics/9255e7a839b771ce20808a0fcd4a1892]

Content:
Every [MATH: k]‑regular directed graph can be converted into a [MATH: 2k]‑regular undirected graph by replacing each of its directed edges with an undirected edge.

Content:
For example, if we replace directed edges with undirected edges in the [MATH: 2]-regular directed graph above (on the left), we obtain a [MATH: 4]-regular undirected graph. Similarly, if we replace directed edges with undirected edges in the [MATH: 1]-regular directed graph above (on the right), we obtain a [MATH: 2]-regular undirected graph.

If [MATH: E] is the set of all edges in a [MATH: k]-regular directed graph with [MATH: n] vertices, then the number of edges can be calculated using the following formula:
[MATH: |E|=n \cdot k]

Content:
Indeed, there are [MATH: n] vertices, each connected by [MATH: k] incoming and [MATH: k] outgoing edges, i.e., [MATH: 2k] per vertex in total. Since each edge contributes exactly [MATH: 2] to the total sum (as every edge connects two vertices), we need to divide [MATH: n\cdot 2k] by [MATH: 2.]

sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

The number of edges in a [MATH: k]-regular directed graph with [MATH: n] vertices is given by

[MATH: |E|= n ⋅ k.]

Substituting the known values [MATH: |E|=12] and [MATH: K=2] into the formula above and solving for [MATH: n,] we get

[MATH: 12|= n ⋅ 2; n|= (12)/(2); n|= 6.]

Therefore, a [MATH: 2]-regular directed graph with [MATH: 12] edges has [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}6}] vertices.

Item 8 — Tutorial: Regular Directed Graphs

Content:
Recall that, in a directed graph [MATH: G=(V,E),] the indegree of a vertex is the number of incoming edges, while the outdegree is the number of outgoing edges.

Content:
A directed graph is called a regular directed graph if all its vertices have the same indegree and outdegree, and [MATH: k]-regular if that degree is [MATH: k]. In other words, a [MATH: k]-regular directed graph satisfies
[MATH: \deg^-(v_i)=\deg^+(v_i)=k]
for all [MATH: v_i\in V] and some fixed constant [MATH: k,] and a regular directed graph is a directed graph which is [MATH: k]-regular for some [MATH: k].

For example, consider the regular directed graphs shown below: in the graph on the left, each vertex has an indegree and an outdegree of [MATH: 2,] while in the graph on the right, each vertex has an indegree and an outdegree of [MATH: 1.]
